title: Exam 4 Numbers to Know
description: Exam 4 drill, matched to the instructor's study guide: the numbers to know, from the diabetes, cholesterol, and metabolic syndrome cutoffs to the blood gas ranges, capillary refill, the QRS, the lungs' lobes and segments, and more. Most questions show a new number on every attempt.

questions.stem: A client's fasting plasma glucose is {g} mg/dL. Which range is this result in?
questions.rationale:
A fasting plasma glucose of 126 mg/dL or higher is in the diabetes range; {g} mg/dL is over that line.

Prediabetes isn't the right answer, even when the number is close to the line: prediabetes stops at 125.

Takeaway: Fasting glucose: under 100 normal, 100 to 125 prediabetes, 126 or higher diabetes; under 70 is low.

questions.stem: A client's fasting plasma glucose is {g} mg/dL. Which range is this result in?
questions.rationale:
A fasting glucose of 100 to 125 mg/dL is prediabetes; {g} mg/dL falls in it.

Normal isn't the right answer: the number is close to 100, but normal is under 100.

Takeaway: Fasting glucose: under 100 normal, 100 to 125 prediabetes, 126 or higher diabetes; under 70 is low.

questions.stem: A client's fasting plasma glucose is {g} mg/dL. Which range is this result in?
questions.rationale:
A fasting glucose under 100 mg/dL (and at least 70) is normal; {g} mg/dL is in that range.

Prediabetes isn't the right answer, even when the number is in the high 90s: prediabetes starts at 100.

Takeaway: Fasting glucose: under 100 normal, 100 to 125 prediabetes, 126 or higher diabetes; under 70 is low.

questions.stem: A client's hemoglobin A1C is {a}%. Which range is this result in?
questions.rationale:
An A1C of 6.5% or higher is in the diabetes range; {a}% is at or over that line.

Prediabetes isn't the right answer, even for a number just over 6.4: 6.5% is already diabetes.

Takeaway: A1C: under 5.7% normal, 5.7% to 6.4% prediabetes, 6.5% or higher diabetes.

questions.stem: A client's hemoglobin A1C is {a}%. Which range is this result in?
questions.rationale:
An A1C of 5.7% to 6.4% is prediabetes, and the instructor's guide lists an A1C over 5.7% as a risk factor for diabetes; {a}% is in that range.

Normal isn't the right answer: the number is under 6.5, but normal is under 5.7%.

Takeaway: A1C: under 5.7% normal, 5.7% to 6.4% prediabetes, 6.5% or higher diabetes.

questions.stem: A client's hemoglobin A1C is {a}%. Which range is this result in?
questions.rationale:
An A1C under 5.7% is normal; {a}% is in that range.

Prediabetes isn't the right answer, even when the number is in the mid-5s: prediabetes starts at 5.7%.

Takeaway: A1C: under 5.7% normal, 5.7% to 6.4% prediabetes, 6.5% or higher diabetes.

questions.stem: Two hours after a 75-g glucose drink, a client's glucose is {g} mg/dL. Which range is this result in?
questions.rationale:
Two hours after the glucose drink, 200 mg/dL or higher is in the diabetes range; {g} mg/dL is at or over it.

Prediabetes isn't the right answer. The fasting cutoffs are lower, but the 2-hour test has its own: 140 to 199 is prediabetes.

Takeaway: 2-hour glucose: under 140 normal, 140 to 199 prediabetes, 200 or higher diabetes.

questions.stem: Two hours after a 75-g glucose drink, a client's glucose is {g} mg/dL. Which range is this result in?
questions.rationale:
Two hours after the glucose drink, 140 to 199 mg/dL is prediabetes; {g} mg/dL falls in it.

The diabetes range isn't the right answer: {g} is well over the fasting cutoff of 126, but the 2-hour test's diabetes line is 200.

Takeaway: 2-hour glucose: under 140 normal, 140 to 199 prediabetes, 200 or higher diabetes.

questions.stem: A client who is sweaty and shaky has a fingerstick glucose of {g} mg/dL. Which range is this result in?
questions.rationale:
A glucose under 70 mg/dL is low (hypoglycemia), and sweating and shakiness are its classic signs; {g} mg/dL is in that range.

The normal range isn't the right answer, even for a number in the 60s: normal starts at 70.

Takeaway: Under 70 mg/dL is hypoglycemia: treat it quickly.

questions.stem: A client with constant thirst and frequent urination has a random glucose of {g} mg/dL. How should the nurse interpret this result?
options: It needs a fasting test before it can mean anything
It's normal for a sample taken at a random time
It's in the prediabetes range, since it wasn't fasting
It's in the diabetes range, since the client has symptoms
questions.rationale:
A random glucose of 200 mg/dL or higher with classic symptoms (thirst, frequent urination, weight loss) meets the criteria for diabetes; {g} mg/dL with these symptoms does.

Needing a fasting test isn't the right answer: one random result usually isn't enough, but symptoms plus a random glucose of 200 or more is one of the four criteria.

Takeaway: Random glucose 200 or higher with symptoms = diabetes range.

questions.stem: A client's total cholesterol is {tc} mg/dL. How should the nurse interpret this result?
options: Borderline, but not yet a risk factor
A risk factor for heart disease
Too low, a sign of poor nutrition
questions.rationale:
The instructor's guide lists a total cholesterol over 200 mg/dL as a risk factor for cardiovascular disease; {tc} mg/dL is over it.

Borderline isn't the right answer, even for a number just over 200. The guide's line is 200: anything over it counts.

Takeaway: Risk factors: total cholesterol over 200, LDL over 100, HDL under 40 (men) or 50 (women).

questions.stem: A client's total cholesterol is {tc} mg/dL. How should the nurse interpret this result?
options: A risk factor for heart disease
Borderline, but not yet a risk factor
Too low, a sign of poor nutrition
questions.rationale:
A total cholesterol under 200 mg/dL isn't a risk factor by the instructor's cutoff; {tc} mg/dL is under it.

A risk factor isn't the right answer, even when the number is in the 190s: the line is 200.

Takeaway: Risk factors: total cholesterol over 200, LDL over 100, HDL under 40 (men) or 50 (women).

questions.stem: A client's LDL is {ldl} mg/dL. How should the nurse interpret this result?
options: A risk factor for heart disease
Borderline, but not yet a risk factor
Too low, a sign of poor nutrition
questions.rationale:
An LDL over 100 mg/dL is a risk factor for cardiovascular disease; {ldl} mg/dL is over it.

Within the desired range isn't the right answer: it would be with the total cholesterol line (200), but LDL has its own line, 100.

Takeaway: Risk factors: total cholesterol over 200, LDL over 100, HDL under 40 (men) or 50 (women).

questions.stem: A client's LDL is {ldl} mg/dL. How should the nurse interpret this result?
options: A risk factor for heart disease
Borderline, but not yet a risk factor
Too low, a sign of poor nutrition
questions.rationale:
An LDL under 100 mg/dL isn't a risk factor by the instructor's cutoff; {ldl} mg/dL is under it.

Too low isn't the right answer, even for a low number: a low LDL is the goal, not a problem.

Takeaway: Risk factors: total cholesterol over 200, LDL over 100, HDL under 40 (men) or 50 (women).

questions.stem: A woman's HDL is {hdl} mg/dL. How should the nurse interpret this result?
options: A risk factor for heart disease
Borderline, but not yet a risk factor
Too low, a sign of poor nutrition
questions.rationale:
For women, an HDL under 50 mg/dL is a risk factor; {hdl} mg/dL is under it.

Within the desired range isn't the right answer: it would be with the men's line (40), but for women the line is 50.

Takeaway: Risk factors: total cholesterol over 200, LDL over 100, HDL under 40 (men) or 50 (women).

questions.stem: A man's HDL is {hdl} mg/dL. How should the nurse interpret this result?
options: A risk factor for heart disease
Borderline, but not yet a risk factor
Too low, a sign of poor nutrition
questions.rationale:
For men, an HDL under 40 mg/dL is a risk factor; {hdl} mg/dL is above it, so it isn't one.

A risk factor isn't the right answer: it would be with the women's line (50), but for men the line is 40.

Takeaway: Risk factors: total cholesterol over 200, LDL over 100, HDL under 40 (men) or 50 (women).

questions.stem: A client's body mass index (BMI) is {b}. How should the nurse interpret it?
options: A risk factor for diabetes and heart disease
Not a risk factor for either disease
A sign of malnutrition and weight loss
A risk factor for diabetes but not heart disease
questions.rationale:
The instructor's guide lists a BMI over 25 as a risk factor for both diabetes and cardiovascular disease; {b} is over it.

A risk factor for diabetes but not heart disease isn't the right answer: BMI comes up in diabetes screening, but the guide lists it for heart disease too.

Takeaway: BMI over 25: a risk factor for diabetes and cardiovascular disease.

questions.stem: A client's body mass index (BMI) is {b}. How should the nurse interpret it?
options: Not a risk factor for either disease
A risk factor for diabetes and heart disease
A sign of malnutrition and weight loss
A risk factor for diabetes but not heart disease
questions.rationale:
A BMI of 25 or under isn't on the instructor's list of risk factors; {b} is under it.

A risk factor isn't the right answer, even when the number is close to 25: the line is over 25.

Takeaway: BMI over 25: a risk factor for diabetes and cardiovascular disease.

questions.stem: A man's waist is {w} in., his triglycerides are {tg} mg/dL, his HDL is {hdl} mg/dL, his blood pressure is {sbp}/{dbp} mm Hg, and his fasting glucose is {fg} mg/dL. How many metabolic syndrome criteria does he meet?
options: 1, so he doesn't have metabolic syndrome
2, so he doesn't have metabolic syndrome
questions.rationale:
He meets two: a waist of {w} in. (about 40 or more for men) and triglycerides of {tg} (150 or more). His HDL of {hdl} isn't low for a man (under 40), his blood pressure is under 130/85, and his glucose is under 100. Metabolic syndrome needs 3 or more.

3 isn't the right answer: it counts his HDL as low, but for men the line is 40.

Takeaway: Metabolic syndrome: 3 or more of waist, triglycerides, low HDL, blood pressure, fasting glucose.

questions.stem: A woman's waist is {w} in., her triglycerides are {tg} mg/dL, her HDL is {hdl} mg/dL, her blood pressure is {sbp}/{dbp} mm Hg, and her fasting glucose is {fg} mg/dL. How many metabolic syndrome criteria does she meet?
options: 2, so she doesn't have metabolic syndrome
1, so she doesn't have metabolic syndrome
questions.rationale:
She meets three: a waist of {w} in. (35 or more for women), an HDL of {hdl} (under 50 for women), and a blood pressure of {sbp}/{dbp} (130/85 or more). Her triglycerides are under 150 and her glucose under 100. Three criteria means metabolic syndrome.

2 isn't the right answer: it uses the men's HDL line (40), which would make her HDL normal.

Takeaway: Metabolic syndrome: 3 or more of waist, triglycerides, low HDL, blood pressure, fasting glucose.

questions.stem: A nurse checks a client's capillary refill, and the color returns in {s} seconds. How should the nurse interpret this?
options: Normal: blood flow to the tissues is good
Slow, but expected in any older adult
Slow: blood flow to the tissues is reduced
Too fast, a sign of high blood pressure
questions.rationale:
Capillary refill measures peripheral perfusion. Color should return in about 2 seconds (no more than 3); {s} seconds is slow, so blood flow to the tissues is reduced.

Expected in older adults isn't the right answer: a slow refill needs follow-up at any age.

Takeaway: Capillary refill: about 2 seconds, no more than 3.

questions.stem: A nurse checks a client's capillary refill, and the color returns in {s} seconds. How should the nurse interpret this?
options: Slow: blood flow to the tissues is reduced
Slow, but expected in any older adult
Too fast, a sign of high blood pressure
Normal: blood flow to the tissues is good
questions.rationale:
Color returning in about 2 seconds or less shows good blood flow to the tissues; {s} seconds is normal.

Too fast isn't the right answer: quick sounds abnormal, but a quick refill just means good perfusion.

Takeaway: Capillary refill: about 2 seconds, no more than 3.

questions.stem: A client's QRS complex measures {q} seconds on the ECG. How should the nurse interpret this?
options: Normal for a P wave, not a QRS
questions.rationale:
The QRS shows the ventricles depolarizing and is normally under 0.12 seconds (120 ms); {q} seconds is wide, so the ventricles are depolarizing slowly: report it.

Within the normal width isn't the right answer: the number is small, but the QRS line is 0.12.

Takeaway: QRS under 0.12 seconds is normal; wider needs follow-up.

questions.stem: A client's QRS complex measures {q} seconds on the ECG. How should the nurse interpret this?
options: Normal for a P wave, not a QRS
questions.rationale:
A QRS under 0.12 seconds is normal; {q} seconds is within it.

Narrower than normal isn't the right answer, even for a small number: a narrow QRS is the normal finding.

Takeaway: QRS under 0.12 seconds is normal; wider needs follow-up.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing the blood. Complete the following sentence.
questions.text: Plasma makes up about {{0}} of the blood, and red blood cells live about {{1}}.
questions.rationale:
Plasma, the liquid part (mostly water, with salts, proteins, hormones, and vitamins), is about 55% of the blood; the formed elements are about 45%. Red cells live about 120 days.

90% isn't the right answer: that's about how much of the plasma is water.

Takeaway: Plasma about 55%; red cells live about 120 days.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing normal arterial blood gases. Complete the following sentence.
questions.text: A normal pH is {{0}}, a normal PaCO₂ is {{1}}, and a normal HCO₃⁻ is {{2}}.
questions.rationale:
Normal: pH 7.35–7.45, PaCO₂ 35–45 mm Hg, HCO₃⁻ 22–26 mEq/L.

80 to 100 isn't the right answer for the PaCO₂: that's the normal PaO₂ (oxygen).

Takeaway: pH 7.35–7.45, PaCO₂ 35–45, HCO₃⁻ 22–26.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing normal arterial blood gases. Complete the following sentence.
questions.text: A normal PaO₂ is {{0}}, and a normal base excess is {{1}}.
questions.rationale:
Normal: PaO₂ 80–100 mm Hg and base excess −2 to +2 mEq/L. Below −2 means too little base (metabolic acidosis); above +2, too much (metabolic alkalosis).

A base excess range of 0 to +4 isn't the right answer, even though “excess” sounds positive; normal is centered on zero.

Takeaway: PaO₂ 80–100; base excess −2 to +2.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing the lungs. Complete the following sentence.
questions.text: The right lung has {{0}} lobes and {{1}} segments; the left lung has {{2}} lobes and {{3}} segments.
questions.rationale:
Right lung: 3 lobes, 10 segments. Left lung: 2 lobes, 8 to 9 segments, leaving room for the heart.

Giving the left lung 3 lobes is a mistake; the lingula is part of the left upper lobe.

Takeaway: Right 3 and 10; left 2 and 8 to 9.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old client breathing room air has a PaO₂ of {p} mm Hg. How should the nurse interpret this value?
options: It can't be judged without the pH
questions.rationale:
A normal PaO₂ is 80 to 100 mm Hg; {p} is below it, so the blood is carrying too little oxygen.

It can't be judged without the pH isn't the right answer: blood gases are read together, but each value has its own normal range.

Takeaway: PaO₂ 80 to 100 mm Hg.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old client breathing room air has a PaO₂ of {p} mm Hg. How should the nurse interpret this value?
options: It can't be judged without the pH
questions.rationale:
A normal PaO₂ is 80 to 100 mm Hg; {p} is within it.

Below the normal range isn't the right answer, even for a number in the 80s: normal starts at 80.

Takeaway: PaO₂ 80 to 100 mm Hg.

questions.stem: A client's phrenic nerve, which controls the diaphragm, was injured. From which level of the spinal cord does this nerve come?
questions.rationale:
The phrenic nerve comes from C3 to C5 in the neck, which is why a high neck injury can stop the diaphragm.

T1 to T4 isn't the right answer: the diaphragm sits in the trunk, but its nerve starts high in the neck.

Takeaway: “C3, 4, 5 keeps the diaphragm alive.”

questions.stem: A client walks {m} minutes on {d} days a week. How many more minutes a week does the client need to reach the goal of 150 minutes?
questions.rationale:
The client walks {m} × {d} = {=m * d} minutes a week. The instructor's goal is 150 minutes a week (for example 20 to 30 minutes on 5 to 7 days), so the client needs 150 − {=m * d} = {answer} more minutes.

Subtracting the daily minutes ({m}) instead of the weekly total is a mistake.

Takeaway: Exercise goal: about 150 minutes a week.

questions.stem: A client's TSH is {t} mIU/L (normal about 0.4 to 4.0). Which condition does this result suggest?
options: A problem with the parathyroid glands
questions.rationale:
TSH is the pituitary's signal to the thyroid. A high TSH ({t}) means the pituitary is pushing harder because the thyroid isn't keeping up: an underactive thyroid.

An overactive thyroid isn't the right answer: a high number sounds like “too much”, but a high TSH usually means too little thyroid hormone.

Takeaway: High TSH: underactive thyroid. Low TSH: overactive thyroid.

questions.stem: A client's TSH is {t} mIU/L (normal about 0.4 to 4.0). Which condition does this result suggest?
options: A problem with the parathyroid glands
questions.rationale:
A low TSH ({t}) means the pituitary has backed off because there's plenty of thyroid hormone: an overactive thyroid.

An underactive thyroid isn't the right answer: a low number sounds like “too little”, but the thyroid hormone itself is high.

Takeaway: High TSH: underactive thyroid. Low TSH: overactive thyroid.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing the stages of inflammation. Complete the following sentence.
questions.text: Acute inflammation lasts {{0}}, subacute inflammation lasts about {{1}}, and chronic inflammation lasts {{2}}.
questions.rationale:
Acute inflammation starts within minutes to hours and lasts days; subacute lasts about 2 to 6 weeks; chronic lasts months or longer.

2 to 6 days isn't the right answer for subacute: that's still the acute stage.

Takeaway: Acute: days. Subacute: 2 to 6 weeks. Chronic: months or longer.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing immunity. Complete the following sentence.
questions.text: The first specific (adaptive) response to a new germ takes about {{0}}, the flu vaccine is given {{1}}, and adults should exercise about {{2}} a week.
questions.rationale:
The adaptive response to a new germ takes about 4 to 7 days to build. The flu vaccine is given every year (the viruses change), and the exercise goal is about 150 minutes a week.

1 to 2 days isn't the right answer: that's how fast the innate defenses (like inflammation) respond.

Takeaway: Adaptive response 4 to 7 days; flu vaccine yearly; exercise 150 minutes a week.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing cortisol. Complete the following sentence.
questions.text: Cortisol is highest in the {{0}} and lowest around {{1}}, so a blood test is usually drawn at about {{2}}.
questions.rationale:
Cortisol follows a daily rhythm: highest in the early morning, lowest around midnight. A morning blood test (about 8 a.m.) catches the peak.

The evening isn't the right answer, even though people often feel most stressed then; cortisol is actually falling at that time.

Takeaway: Cortisol: high in the morning, low at midnight.

questions.stem: A client's fasting plasma glucose is {g} mg/dL, and the client's A1C is {a}%. How should the nurse interpret these results?
options: The A1C is in the diabetes range; the fasting glucose is in the prediabetes range
Both results are in the diabetes range
Both results are in the prediabetes range
The fasting glucose is in the diabetes range; the A1C is in the prediabetes range
questions.rationale:
An A1C of {a}% is 6.5% or higher: diabetes. A fasting glucose of {g} mg/dL is 100 to 125: prediabetes. Each test is read against its own cutoffs.

Both in the diabetes range: the fasting line for diabetes is 126, and {g} is under it. Both in the prediabetes range: the A1C's prediabetes range stops at 6.4%. The fasting glucose in the diabetes range swaps the two results.

Takeaway: Fasting: under 100 normal, 100 to 125 prediabetes, 126 or higher diabetes. A1C: under 5.7% normal, 5.7% to 6.4% prediabetes, 6.5% or higher diabetes. 2-hour: under 140, 140 to 199, 200 or higher.

questions.stem: A client's 2-hour glucose tolerance result is {g} mg/dL, and the fasting glucose was {f} mg/dL. How should the nurse interpret these results?
options: The 2-hour result is in the prediabetes range; the fasting result is normal
The 2-hour result is in the diabetes range; the fasting result is normal
Both results are in the prediabetes range
questions.rationale:
Two hours after the glucose drink, 140 to 199 is prediabetes, so {g} mg/dL is prediabetes. A fasting glucose of {f} is under 100: normal.

Both normal: the 2-hour normal line is under 140. The 2-hour result in the diabetes range: its diabetes line is 200, not the fasting 126. Both prediabetes: the fasting result is under 100.

Takeaway: Fasting: under 100 normal, 100 to 125 prediabetes, 126 or higher diabetes. A1C: under 5.7% normal, 5.7% to 6.4% prediabetes, 6.5% or higher diabetes. 2-hour: under 140, 140 to 199, 200 or higher.

questions.stem: A client's fasting glucose was {g1} mg/dL last month and is {g2} mg/dL today. Which change should the nurse recognize?
options: It moved from the normal range into the prediabetes range
It stayed in the diabetes range
It moved from the prediabetes range into the diabetes range
It stayed in the prediabetes range
questions.rationale:
A fasting glucose of {g1} mg/dL is prediabetes (100 to 125); {g2} mg/dL is 126 or higher: diabetes. The client crossed the line.

Stayed in the prediabetes range: the range stops at 125. From normal into prediabetes: normal is under 100, and {g1} isn't. Stayed in the diabetes range: {g1} was under 126.

Takeaway: Fasting: under 100 normal, 100 to 125 prediabetes, 126 or higher diabetes. A1C: under 5.7% normal, 5.7% to 6.4% prediabetes, 6.5% or higher diabetes. 2-hour: under 140, 140 to 199, 200 or higher.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing four clients' laboratory results. Which result should the nurse recognize as meeting a criterion for diabetes?
options: Random glucose 212 mg/dL, with constant thirst
questions.rationale:
A random glucose of 200 or higher with symptoms (thirst, frequent urination, weight loss) is one of the criteria for diabetes.

The other three sit one step below their diabetes lines: fasting 125 (the line is 126), A1C 6.4% (6.5%), and 2-hour 198 (200). Each is prediabetes, and symptoms don't change that: only the random test counts symptoms.

Takeaway: Fasting: under 100 normal, 100 to 125 prediabetes, 126 or higher diabetes. A1C: under 5.7% normal, 5.7% to 6.4% prediabetes, 6.5% or higher diabetes. 2-hour: under 140, 140 to 199, 200 or higher.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing four clients' laboratory results. Which result should the nurse recognize as meeting a criterion for diabetes?
options: A random glucose of 230 mg/dL with no symptoms
questions.rationale:
An A1C of 6.5% is exactly the diabetes line, and the line counts: 6.5% or higher.

Fasting 124 and 2-hour 196 are prediabetes. A random glucose of 230 without symptoms isn't a criterion by itself: the random test counts with classic symptoms.

Takeaway: Fasting: under 100 normal, 100 to 125 prediabetes, 126 or higher diabetes. A1C: under 5.7% normal, 5.7% to 6.4% prediabetes, 6.5% or higher diabetes. 2-hour: under 140, 140 to 199, 200 or higher.

questions.stem: A client who just ate a large holiday meal has a random glucose of {g} mg/dL and no thirst, frequent urination, or weight loss. How should the nurse interpret this result?
options: It meets the criteria for diabetes, since it's over 200
It's in the prediabetes range for a random test
It's normal for a sample taken after a meal
It doesn't meet the criteria by itself; it needs a confirming test
questions.rationale:
A random glucose of 200 or higher meets the criteria only with classic symptoms. Without them, {g} mg/dL right after a big meal needs a confirming test (fasting glucose, A1C, or a 2-hour test).

It meets the criteria leaves out the symptoms the random test needs. Prediabetes for a random test: the random test has no prediabetes range. Normal after a meal: over 200 is high at any time.

Takeaway: Fasting: under 100 normal, 100 to 125 prediabetes, 126 or higher diabetes. A1C: under 5.7% normal, 5.7% to 6.4% prediabetes, 6.5% or higher diabetes. 2-hour: under 140, 140 to 199, 200 or higher.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing clients' results. Which results should the nurse recognize as in the prediabetes range? Select all that apply.
questions.rationale:
Prediabetes starts exactly at fasting 100, A1C 5.7%, and 2-hour 140.

Fasting 99 is still normal. A1C 6.5% and 2-hour 200 are the diabetes lines.

Takeaway: Fasting: under 100 normal, 100 to 125 prediabetes, 126 or higher diabetes. A1C: under 5.7% normal, 5.7% to 6.4% prediabetes, 6.5% or higher diabetes. 2-hour: under 140, 140 to 199, 200 or higher.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing clients' results. Which results should the nurse report as meeting the criteria for diabetes? Select all that apply.
options: An A1C of 6.4% on two tests
A random glucose of 210 mg/dL with thirst
A random glucose of 240 mg/dL with no symptoms
questions.rationale:
Fasting 126 and 2-hour 200 are exactly on the diabetes lines, which count. A random 210 with thirst, a classic symptom, meets the random criterion.

A1C 6.4% and fasting 125 are the top of the prediabetes ranges. Random 240 with no symptoms needs a confirming test.

Takeaway: Fasting: under 100 normal, 100 to 125 prediabetes, 126 or higher diabetes. A1C: under 5.7% normal, 5.7% to 6.4% prediabetes, 6.5% or higher diabetes. 2-hour: under 140, 140 to 199, 200 or higher.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing a client's results over time. For each result, specify how the nurse should interpret it.
questions.rationale:
Fasting 99: normal (under 100). A1C 6.5%: diabetes (6.5% or higher). 2-hour 139: normal (under 140). Fasting 100: prediabetes (100 to 125). A1C 5.6%: normal (under 5.7%).

The rows most often missed sit right on a line: 100 and 6.5% are already in the next range, while 99, 139, and 5.6% are not.

Takeaway: Fasting: under 100 normal, 100 to 125 prediabetes, 126 or higher diabetes. A1C: under 5.7% normal, 5.7% to 6.4% prediabetes, 6.5% or higher diabetes. 2-hour: under 140, 140 to 199, 200 or higher.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing several clients' results. For each result, specify how the nurse should interpret it.
questions.rationale:
2-hour 140 and A1C 5.7%: the first values of prediabetes. A1C 6.4%: the last value of prediabetes. Fasting 126 and 2-hour 200: the diabetes lines, which count.

The 2-hour and fasting tests have different lines: 140 is high two hours after the drink but would be diabetes if fasting.

Takeaway: Fasting: under 100 normal, 100 to 125 prediabetes, 126 or higher diabetes. A1C: under 5.7% normal, 5.7% to 6.4% prediabetes, 6.5% or higher diabetes. 2-hour: under 140, 140 to 199, 200 or higher.

questions.stem: A nurse is checking fingerstick glucose results for four clients. Which result should the nurse treat as hypoglycemia?
questions.rationale:
Hypoglycemia is a glucose under 70 mg/dL: 69 is below the line.

70 is the bottom of the normal range, not below it. 74 and 99 are normal.

Takeaway: Under 70 mg/dL is hypoglycemia: treat it quickly.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing a client's history. Which findings should the nurse identify as risk factors for diabetes? Select all that apply.
questions.rationale:
The instructor's risk factors for diabetes: a history of gestational diabetes, an A1C over 5.7%, and a BMI over 25.

BMI 24 and A1C 5.5% are under those lines. A total cholesterol of 212 is a risk factor for cardiovascular disease, not one of the guide's risk factors for diabetes.

Takeaway: Diabetes risk factors: gestational diabetes, A1C over 5.7%, BMI over 25.

questions.stem: A woman whose A1C is {a}% and BMI is {b} had diabetes during a past pregnancy. How many risk factors for diabetes should the nurse identify?
questions.rationale:
All three: a history of gestational diabetes, an A1C over 5.7% ({a}%), and a BMI over 25 ({b}).

2 leaves out the past pregnancy, which counts as gestational diabetes. 1 and 0 treat her A1C or BMI as normal, though both are past the guide's lines.

Takeaway: Diabetes risk factors: gestational diabetes, A1C over 5.7%, BMI over 25.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing the criteria for diabetes. Complete the following sentence.
questions.text: A fasting glucose of {{0}} or higher, an A1C of {{1}} or higher, or a 2-hour glucose of {{2}} or higher meets the criteria for diabetes.
questions.rationale:
Diabetes: fasting 126, A1C 6.5%, or 2-hour 200 or higher (or a random 200 or higher with symptoms).

100, 5.7%, and 140 are where prediabetes starts.

Takeaway: Fasting: under 100 normal, 100 to 125 prediabetes, 126 or higher diabetes. A1C: under 5.7% normal, 5.7% to 6.4% prediabetes, 6.5% or higher diabetes. 2-hour: under 140, 140 to 199, 200 or higher.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing prediabetes. Complete the following sentence.
questions.text: Prediabetes is a fasting glucose of {{0}}, or an A1C of {{1}}.
questions.rationale:
Prediabetes: fasting 100 to 125, A1C 5.7% to 6.4% (and a 2-hour glucose of 140 to 199).

70 to 99 and 4.0% to 5.6% are normal; 126 and up and 6.5% and up are diabetes.

Takeaway: Fasting: under 100 normal, 100 to 125 prediabetes, 126 or higher diabetes. A1C: under 5.7% normal, 5.7% to 6.4% prediabetes, 6.5% or higher diabetes. 2-hour: under 140, 140 to 199, 200 or higher.

questions.stem: A client's A1C was {a1}% six months ago and is {a2}% today. Which change should the nurse recognize?
options: It moved from the prediabetes range into the diabetes range
It stayed in the prediabetes range
It moved from the normal range into the prediabetes range
It stayed in the normal range
questions.rationale:
An A1C of {a1}% is normal (under 5.7%); {a2}% is prediabetes (5.7% to 6.4%).

Stayed normal: normal stops below 5.7%. Into the diabetes range: that starts at 6.5%. Stayed prediabetes: {a1}% was still normal.

Takeaway: Fasting: under 100 normal, 100 to 125 prediabetes, 126 or higher diabetes. A1C: under 5.7% normal, 5.7% to 6.4% prediabetes, 6.5% or higher diabetes. 2-hour: under 140, 140 to 199, 200 or higher.

questions.stem: A client's total cholesterol is {v} mg/dL. How should the nurse interpret this result?
options: Too low, a sign of poor nutrition
A risk factor for heart disease
Borderline, but not yet a risk factor
questions.rationale:
The instructor's line is over 200: {v} mg/dL isn't over it, so it isn't a risk factor.

A risk factor: the number sits right at the line, but the line says over (or under), and this value isn't past it. Borderline: the guide has no borderline zone; a value is past the line or it isn't. Too low: nothing here is low.

Takeaway: Risk factors: total cholesterol over 200, LDL over 100, HDL under 40 (men) or under 50 (women), BMI over 25. A value exactly on the line isn't over it.

questions.stem: A client's LDL is {v} mg/dL. How should the nurse interpret this result?
options: A risk factor for heart disease
Borderline, but not yet a risk factor
Too low, a sign of poor nutrition
questions.rationale:
The line for LDL is over 100: {v} mg/dL isn't over it, so it isn't a risk factor.

A risk factor: the number sits right at the line, but the line says over (or under), and this value isn't past it. Borderline: the guide has no borderline zone; a value is past the line or it isn't. Too low: nothing here is low.

Takeaway: Risk factors: total cholesterol over 200, LDL over 100, HDL under 40 (men) or under 50 (women), BMI over 25. A value exactly on the line isn't over it.

questions.stem: A man's HDL is {v} mg/dL. How should the nurse interpret this result?
options: A risk factor for heart disease
Borderline, but not yet a risk factor
Too low, a sign of poor nutrition
questions.rationale:
For men, an HDL under 40 is the risk factor: {v} mg/dL isn't under it.

A risk factor: the number sits right at the line, but the line says over (or under), and this value isn't past it. Borderline: the guide has no borderline zone; a value is past the line or it isn't. Too low: nothing here is low.

Takeaway: Risk factors: total cholesterol over 200, LDL over 100, HDL under 40 (men) or under 50 (women), BMI over 25. A value exactly on the line isn't over it.

questions.stem: A woman's HDL is {v} mg/dL. How should the nurse interpret this result?
options: Borderline, but not yet a risk factor
Too low, a sign of poor nutrition
A risk factor for heart disease
questions.rationale:
For women, an HDL under 50 is the risk factor: {v} mg/dL isn't under it.

A risk factor: the number sits right at the line, but the line says over (or under), and this value isn't past it. Borderline: the guide has no borderline zone; a value is past the line or it isn't. Too low: nothing here is low.

Takeaway: Risk factors: total cholesterol over 200, LDL over 100, HDL under 40 (men) or under 50 (women), BMI over 25. A value exactly on the line isn't over it.

questions.stem: A client's body mass index (BMI) is {v}. How should the nurse interpret it for heart disease risk?
options: Too low, a sign of poor nutrition
A risk factor for heart disease
Borderline, but not yet a risk factor
questions.rationale:
The guide's risk factor is a BMI over 25: {v} isn't over it.

A risk factor: the number sits right at the line, but the line says over (or under), and this value isn't past it. Borderline: the guide has no borderline zone; a value is past the line or it isn't. Too low: nothing here is low.

Takeaway: Risk factors: total cholesterol over 200, LDL over 100, HDL under 40 (men) or under 50 (women), BMI over 25. A value exactly on the line isn't over it.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man's results: total cholesterol 196 mg/dL, LDL 108 mg/dL, HDL 43 mg/dL, and BMI 24. He doesn't smoke. Which result should the nurse identify as a risk factor for cardiovascular disease?
questions.rationale:
An LDL over 100 is a risk factor: 108 is over it.

Total cholesterol 196 is under 200. HDL 43 is above the men's line of 40. BMI 24 is under 25.

Takeaway: Risk factors: total cholesterol over 200, LDL over 100, HDL under 40 (men) or under 50 (women), BMI over 25. A value exactly on the line isn't over it.

questions.stem: A 47-year-old woman's results: total cholesterol 188 mg/dL, LDL 94 mg/dL, HDL 47 mg/dL, and BMI 23. Which result should the nurse identify as a risk factor for cardiovascular disease?
questions.rationale:
For women, an HDL under 50 is a risk factor: 47 is under it.

Total cholesterol 188 is under 200, LDL 94 under 100, and BMI 23 under 25. An HDL of 47 would be fine for a man (line 40), but not for a woman.

Takeaway: Risk factors: total cholesterol over 200, LDL over 100, HDL under 40 (men) or under 50 (women), BMI over 25. A value exactly on the line isn't over it.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman smokes. Her total cholesterol is 214 mg/dL, LDL 96 mg/dL, HDL 46 mg/dL, BMI 27, and blood pressure 118/76 mm Hg. Which findings should the nurse identify as risk factors for cardiovascular disease? Select all that apply.
questions.rationale:
Her risk factors: total cholesterol over 200, an HDL under 50 (the women's line), a BMI over 25, and smoking (age is one too).

LDL 96 is under 100. 118/76 isn't high blood pressure.

Takeaway: Risk factors: total cholesterol over 200, LDL over 100, HDL under 40 (men) or under 50 (women), BMI over 25. A value exactly on the line isn't over it.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man doesn't smoke. His total cholesterol is 203 mg/dL, LDL 112 mg/dL, HDL 46 mg/dL, BMI 25, and he has diabetes. Which findings should the nurse identify as risk factors for cardiovascular disease? Select all that apply.
questions.rationale:
His risk factors: total cholesterol over 200, LDL over 100, diabetes, and age.

HDL 46 is above the men's line of 40. BMI 25 is on the line, not over it.

Takeaway: Risk factors: total cholesterol over 200, LDL over 100, HDL under 40 (men) or under 50 (women), BMI over 25. A value exactly on the line isn't over it.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing results from several clients. For each finding, specify whether it's a risk factor for cardiovascular disease.
rows: An HDL of 45 mg/dL in a man
An HDL of 45 mg/dL in a woman
questions.rationale:
HDL 45 in a man: not a risk factor (line 40). HDL 45 in a woman: a risk factor (line 50). LDL 100: on the line, not over it. Total cholesterol 205 and BMI 25.5: over their lines.

The same HDL can be fine in one client and a risk in another: check the client's sex first.

Takeaway: Risk factors: total cholesterol over 200, LDL over 100, HDL under 40 (men) or under 50 (women), BMI over 25. A value exactly on the line isn't over it.

questions.stem: A man's waist is {w} in., his triglycerides are {tg} mg/dL, his HDL is {hdl} mg/dL, his blood pressure is {sbp}/{dbp} mm Hg, and his fasting glucose is {fg} mg/dL. How many metabolic syndrome criteria should the nurse identify?
options: 1, so he doesn't have metabolic syndrome
2, so he doesn't have metabolic syndrome
questions.rationale:
He meets three: triglycerides of {tg} (150 or more), an HDL of {hdl} (under 40 for men), and a blood pressure of {sbp}/{dbp} (130/85 or more). His waist of {w} in. is under 40, and his glucose of {fg} is under 100. Three criteria means metabolic syndrome.

2 leaves out one of the three he meets. 4 counts his waist or glucose, which are under the lines. 1 counts only one value past its line.

Takeaway: Metabolic syndrome: 3 of 5: waist 40 in. or more (men) or 35 (women), triglycerides 150 or more, HDL under 40 (men) or 50 (women), blood pressure 130/85 or more, fasting glucose 100 or more.

questions.stem: A woman's waist is {w} in., her triglycerides are {tg} mg/dL, her HDL is {hdl} mg/dL, her blood pressure is {sbp}/{dbp} mm Hg, and her fasting glucose is {fg} mg/dL. How many metabolic syndrome criteria should the nurse identify?
options: 1, so she doesn't have metabolic syndrome
2, so she doesn't have metabolic syndrome
questions.rationale:
She meets three: a waist of {w} in. (35 or more for women), an HDL of {hdl} (under 50 for women), and a fasting glucose of {fg} (100 or more). Her triglycerides are under 150 and her blood pressure under 130/85.

2 usually comes from using the men's lines (waist 40, HDL 40). 4 counts her triglycerides or blood pressure, which are under the lines. 1 misses two of her criteria.

Takeaway: Metabolic syndrome: 3 of 5, with different waist and HDL lines for women (35 in., 50) and men (40 in., 40).

questions.stem: A nurse is assessing a woman for metabolic syndrome. For each finding, specify whether it meets the criterion.
questions.rationale:
Waist 36 in.: meets it (35 or more for women). Triglycerides 140: under 150. HDL 52: not under 50. 132/86: 130/85 or more. Fasting glucose 104: 100 or more. She meets three, so she has metabolic syndrome.

The women's lines are lower for the waist (35 in.) and higher for the HDL (50) than the men's.

Takeaway: Metabolic syndrome needs 3 of the 5 criteria.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing the criteria for metabolic syndrome. Complete the following sentence.
questions.text: The criteria include a waist of {{0}} or more in men, triglycerides of {{1}} or more, and a blood pressure of {{2}} or more.
questions.rationale:
Metabolic syndrome: a waist of 40 in. or more in men (35 in women), triglycerides 150 or more, blood pressure 130/85 or more, a low HDL, and a fasting glucose of 100 or more: 3 of the 5.

35 in. is the women's waist line. 200 is the total cholesterol line. 140/90 is higher than the metabolic syndrome line.

Takeaway: Waist 40/35, triglycerides 150, blood pressure 130/85, glucose 100, HDL under 40/50.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing a woman's results. Which findings count toward metabolic syndrome? Select all that apply.
questions.rationale:
Waist 35 in., triglycerides 150, and fasting glucose 100 are exactly on their lines, and these lines count (or more).

HDL 50 isn't under 50. 128/84 is under 130/85. Total cholesterol isn't a metabolic syndrome criterion.

Takeaway: For metabolic syndrome, the waist, triglyceride, blood pressure, and glucose lines include the line itself.

questions.stem: A man meets two metabolic syndrome criteria: triglycerides of 172 mg/dL and a waist of 42 in. Which additional finding would mean he has metabolic syndrome?
options: A blood pressure of 128/82 mm Hg
questions.rationale:
A fasting glucose of 100 or more is the third criterion: 102 completes the three.

HDL 43 isn't low for a man (line 40). 128/82 is under 130/85. Total cholesterol isn't one of the five criteria.

Takeaway: Metabolic syndrome needs 3 of 5, and total cholesterol isn't one of them.

questions.stem: A nurse checks a client's toes. The left foot is cool and pale, its pulses are weak, and color returns in {s} seconds after pressing the nail. Which condition do these findings suggest?
options: Normal circulation in a cool room
A blood clot in a vein of the leg
questions.rationale:
Capillary refill measures blood flow to the tissues. A refill of {s} seconds (normal is about 2, no more than 3), with a cool, pale foot and weak pulses, points to too little arterial blood reaching the foot: arterial insufficiency.

Venous insufficiency brings swelling and brownish skin with a normal refill. A cool room doesn't explain weak pulses in one foot. A clot in a leg vein causes swelling, warmth, and pain, not a slow refill.

Takeaway: Slow refill, cool, pale, weak pulses: arterial. Swelling, brownish skin, normal refill: venous.

questions.stem: A client's lower legs are swollen, with brownish skin near the ankles. The pedal pulses are strong, and color returns in 2 seconds after pressing the nails. Which condition do these findings suggest?
options: Normal findings for an older adult
Reduced blood flow to the toes
questions.rationale:
Swelling and brownish skin with strong pulses and a normal refill (about 2 seconds) point to blood pooling in the veins: venous insufficiency. Arterial blood is still arriving.

Arterial insufficiency would slow the refill and weaken the pulses. Normal for an older adult: swelling and skin changes need follow-up at any age. Reduced blood flow to the toes: a 2-second refill shows good flow.

Takeaway: Capillary refill tests arterial flow: normal refill with swelling points to the veins.

questions.stem: A nurse is teaching a student about capillary refill. Which statement by the student is accurate?
options: "It shows how much oxygen is in the blood, and color should return at once."
"It shows how well blood reaches the tissues, and color should return in about 2 seconds."
"It shows how fast the heart beats, and color should return in about 10 seconds."
"It shows how well the veins drain, and color should return in about 5 seconds."
questions.rationale:
Capillary refill measures peripheral perfusion, blood flow to the tissues: color should return in about 2 seconds (no more than 3).

It doesn't measure the heart rate, venous drainage, or oxygen, and 10 or 5 seconds would be slow.

Takeaway: Capillary refill: perfusion, about 2 seconds, no more than 3.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing the heart. Complete the following sentence.
questions.text: The heart has {{0}} chambers and {{1}} valves.
questions.rationale:
The heart has 4 chambers (two atria, two ventricles) and 4 valves (tricuspid, pulmonic, mitral, aortic).

2 valves counts only the valves between the atria and ventricles, leaving out the two semilunar valves.

Takeaway: 4 chambers, 4 valves.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing the blood. Complete the following sentence.
questions.text: Red blood cells live about {{0}}, and platelets live about {{1}}.
questions.rationale:
Red blood cells live about 120 days; platelets, about 7 to 10 days.

120 days for platelets mixes them up with red cells. 1 to 2 days is closer to how long some white cells last.

Takeaway: Red cells 120 days; platelets 7 to 10 days.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing the electrolytes in plasma. For each electrolyte, specify its charge.
questions.rationale:
The instructor's list: sodium, potassium, calcium, and magnesium are positive; chloride, bicarbonate, and phosphate are negative.

Bicarbonate is the row most often missed: it's a base, but its charge is negative.

Takeaway: Cations: Na⁺, K⁺, Ca²⁺, Mg²⁺. Anions: Cl⁻, HCO₃⁻, phosphate.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing the electrolytes in plasma. Which electrolytes should the nurse identify as positively charged? Select all that apply.
questions.rationale:
Sodium, potassium, magnesium, and calcium are positive ions (cations).

Chloride and bicarbonate are negative ions (anions).

Takeaway: Cations: Na⁺, K⁺, Ca²⁺, Mg²⁺. Anions: Cl⁻, HCO₃⁻, phosphate.

questions.stem: A client's capillary refill is about 1 second in the fingers but 4 seconds in the toes of the left foot only. Which finding should the nurse report?
options: The slow refill in the left toes
The fast refill in the fingers
The difference between the hands and the feet
Nothing: both are within normal limits
questions.rationale:
A refill of 4 seconds is slow (normal is about 2, no more than 3), and in one foot only it suggests reduced arterial flow to that foot: report it.

The fast refill in the fingers is normal. The difference between hands and feet: the problem is the one foot, not the comparison. Nothing: 4 seconds is past the limit.

Takeaway: A slow refill in one limb needs follow-up: it points to that limb's arterial flow.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing the lungs. For each feature, specify the lung it describes.
questions.rationale:
The right lung has 3 lobes and 10 segments; the left lung has 2 lobes and 8 to 9 segments, leaving room for the heart.

Giving the left lung the larger numbers forgets the space the heart takes up.

Takeaway: Right 3 and 10; left 2 and 8 to 9.

questions.stem: A client's chest x-ray shows a pneumonia in the middle lobe. Which lung should the nurse focus on when listening to the client's breath sounds?
options: The lung on the side the client lies on
questions.rationale:
Only the right lung has a middle lobe: it has 3 lobes (upper, middle, lower), and the left has 2.

The left lung has no middle lobe (its lingula is part of the upper lobe). Both lungs and the side the client lies on ignore where the middle lobe is.

Takeaway: Right lung: 3 lobes, including the middle lobe.

questions.stem: A nurse is listening to the breath sounds over each lobe of the lungs. How many lobes does the nurse listen over in all?
questions.rationale:
The right lung has 3 lobes and the left 2: 5 in all.

4 and 6 give the lungs equal lobes. 3 counts only the right lung.

Takeaway: Right 3 + left 2 = 5 lobes.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing four clients' arterial blood gases. Which client's results are entirely within normal limits?
options: pH 7.36, PaCO₂ 44 mm Hg, HCO₃⁻ 21 mEq/L, PaO₂ 96 mm Hg
pH 7.40, PaCO₂ 40 mm Hg, HCO₃⁻ 24 mEq/L, PaO₂ 78 mm Hg
pH 7.45, PaCO₂ 35 mm Hg, HCO₃⁻ 26 mEq/L, PaO₂ 80 mm Hg
pH 7.44, PaCO₂ 34 mm Hg, HCO₃⁻ 25 mEq/L, PaO₂ 90 mm Hg
questions.rationale:
The results with pH 7.45, PaCO₂ 35, HCO₃⁻ 26, and PaO₂ 80 are normal: every value sits on an edge of its range, and the edges are normal.

The others each have one value one step out: a PaCO₂ of 34 (below 35), an HCO₃⁻ of 21 (below 22), and a PaO₂ of 78 (below 80).

Takeaway: pH 7.35–7.45, PaCO₂ 35–45, HCO₃⁻ 22–26, PaO₂ 80–100: the edges count as normal.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing four clients' arterial blood gases. Which client's results are entirely within normal limits?
options: pH 7.39, PaCO₂ 38 mm Hg, HCO₃⁻ 27 mEq/L, PaO₂ 94 mm Hg
pH 7.34, PaCO₂ 42 mm Hg, HCO₃⁻ 23 mEq/L, PaO₂ 88 mm Hg
pH 7.41, PaCO₂ 46 mm Hg, HCO₃⁻ 24 mEq/L, PaO₂ 92 mm Hg
pH 7.35, PaCO₂ 45 mm Hg, HCO₃⁻ 22 mEq/L, PaO₂ 100 mm Hg
questions.rationale:
The results with pH 7.35, PaCO₂ 45, HCO₃⁻ 22, and PaO₂ 100 are normal: every value is on an edge of its range.

The others each miss by one: a pH of 7.34, a PaCO₂ of 46, and an HCO₃⁻ of 27.

Takeaway: pH 7.35–7.45, PaCO₂ 35–45, HCO₃⁻ 22–26, PaO₂ 80–100: the edges count as normal.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing a client's results. Which values should the nurse recognize as within normal limits? Select all that apply.
questions.rationale:
PaO₂ 100, HCO₃⁻ 22, and PaCO₂ 45 are on the edges of their ranges: normal.

pH 7.46, base excess +3, and PaO₂ 79 are one step outside.

Takeaway: pH 7.35–7.45, PaCO₂ 35–45, HCO₃⁻ 22–26, PaO₂ 80–100, base excess −2 to +2.

questions.stem: A client has a spinal cord injury at the level of C2. Which effect on breathing should the nurse anticipate?
options: The diaphragm may stop working, so the client may need a ventilator
Breathing is unaffected, since the injury is above the phrenic nerve's roots
The abdominal muscles used in forced exhaling are the main concern
The scalene and sternocleidomastoid muscles take over without help
questions.rationale:
The phrenic nerve comes from C3 to C5. An injury at C2, above it, cuts the nerve's link to the brain: the diaphragm may stop working, and the client may need a ventilator.

Unaffected: being above the roots is what makes it dangerous. The abdominal muscles are the main concern only with a lower injury. The accessory muscles take over: they can't replace the diaphragm.

Takeaway: “C3, 4, 5 keeps the diaphragm alive”: an injury at or above it threatens breathing.

questions.stem: A client has a spinal cord injury at the level of C7. Which effect on the diaphragm should the nurse anticipate?
options: The diaphragm stops working, so the client needs a ventilator right away
The diaphragm works on the right side but not the left
The diaphragm works during sleep but not while awake
The diaphragm keeps working, since its nerve leaves the cord higher up
questions.rationale:
The phrenic nerve leaves the cord at C3 to C5, above a C7 injury, so the diaphragm keeps working. (Muscles supplied below C7 may be weak.)

Stops working fits an injury at or above C3 to C5. One side and during sleep don't follow from the level of the injury.

Takeaway: Injury below C5: the diaphragm keeps working.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing arterial blood gas ranges. Which range should the nurse expect for a normal PaCO₂?
questions.rationale:
A normal PaCO₂ is 35 to 45 mm Hg.

22 to 26 is the HCO₃⁻, 80 to 100 the PaO₂, and 7.35 to 7.45 the pH.

Takeaway: PaCO₂ 35–45; HCO₃⁻ 22–26; PaO₂ 80–100; pH 7.35–7.45.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing a client's PaO₂. Complete the following sentence.
questions.text: A normal PaO₂ is {{0}}, so a PaO₂ of 76 mm Hg is {{1}}.
questions.rationale:
A normal PaO₂ is 80 to 100 mm Hg; 76 is below it.

35 to 45 is the PaCO₂. 95 to 100 is a normal oxygen saturation in percent, a different measure.

Takeaway: PaO₂ 80–100 mm Hg; oxygen saturation 95% or more.

questions.stem: A client reports weight gain, tiredness, and always feeling cold. The client's TSH is {t} mIU/L (normal about 0.4 to 4.0). Which condition do these findings suggest?
questions.rationale:
A high TSH ({t}) means the pituitary is pushing a thyroid that isn't keeping up, and weight gain, tiredness, and cold intolerance fit: hypothyroidism.

Hyperthyroidism lowers the TSH and brings weight loss and heat intolerance. Normal: {t} is above 4.0. Too much cortisol isn't what the TSH measures.

Takeaway: High TSH: underactive thyroid. Low TSH: overactive thyroid.

questions.stem: A client reports weight loss, a fast heartbeat, and feeling hot all the time. The client's TSH is {t} mIU/L (normal about 0.4 to 4.0). Which condition do these findings suggest?
questions.rationale:
A low TSH ({t}) means the pituitary has backed off because thyroid hormone is high, and weight loss, a fast heartbeat, and heat intolerance fit: hyperthyroidism.

Hypothyroidism raises the TSH. Normal: {t} is below 0.4. A low blood glucose can cause a fast heartbeat, but not a low TSH or constant heat.

Takeaway: High TSH: underactive thyroid. Low TSH: overactive thyroid.

questions.stem: A client's TSH is {t} mIU/L (expected about 0.4 to 4.0). How should the nurse interpret this result?
options: A sign of an underactive thyroid
A sign of an overactive thyroid
Too close to call without a repeat test
questions.rationale:
{t} is within 0.4 to 4.0: a normal TSH.

Underactive would raise it above 4.0; overactive would lower it below 0.4. Too close to call: it's inside the range.

Takeaway: TSH about 0.4 to 4.0 is normal.

questions.stem: A client wants to reach the goal of 150 minutes of exercise a week, exercising on {d} days. How many minutes should each session last?
questions.rationale:
150 minutes ÷ {d} days = {answer} minutes each day, within the instructor's 20 to 30 minutes on 5 to 7 days.

Dividing by 7 when the client exercises on {d} days, or using 150 a day, are the usual mistakes.

Takeaway: Exercise goal: about 150 minutes a week (20 to 30 minutes on 5 to 7 days).

questions.stem: A client walks {m} minutes a day on weekdays only, and nothing on weekends. How many more minutes a week does the client need to reach the goal of 150 minutes?
questions.rationale:
Weekdays only: {m} × 5 = {=m * 5} minutes a week. 150 − {=m * 5} = {answer} more minutes.

Multiplying by 7 counts the weekend days the client doesn't walk.

Takeaway: Exercise goal: about 150 minutes a week.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing clients' exercise plans. Which plan should the nurse recognize as meeting the goal of 150 minutes a week?
questions.rationale:
25 × 6 = 150 minutes: it meets the goal.

40 × 3 = 120, 20 × 5 = 100, and 60 × 1 = 60 all fall short.

Takeaway: Multiply minutes by days: the goal is 150 a week.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing clients' exercise plans. Which plan should the nurse recognize as meeting the goal of 150 minutes a week?
questions.rationale:
30 × 5 = 150 minutes: it meets the goal.

45 × 3 = 135 and 20 × 7 = 140 come close but fall short; 10 × 7 = 70 is half.

Takeaway: Multiply minutes by days: the goal is 150 a week.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing immunizations with a 70-year-old client. Which vaccines should the nurse recommend? Select all that apply.
questions.rationale:
The instructor's list for older adults: pneumococcal and shingles vaccines, plus the annual flu and COVID vaccines, with a record kept of each.

The flu vaccine is given every year, not every 5, since the viruses change. A tetanus booster isn't yearly.

Takeaway: Older adults: pneumococcal and shingles, plus yearly flu and COVID.

questions.stem: A client asks why the influenza vaccine has to be given again this year. Which response by the nurse is accurate?
options: "The flu viruses change, so the vaccine changes each year."
"Last year's vaccine wears off after about six weeks."
"The body can't make memory cells against the flu."
"A yearly dose is meant for people over 65."
questions.rationale:
The vaccine is given every year because the flu viruses change, so a new vaccine is made for the viruses expected that season.

Wears off after six weeks: protection lasts the season. No memory cells: vaccines work by making them. Meant for people over 65: the yearly vaccine is for nearly everyone.

Takeaway: Flu vaccine every year: the viruses change.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing clients with inflammation. For each client, specify the stage the nurse should document.
rows: Redness for 4 days after an injury
questions.rationale:
Acute: minutes to days (2 hours, 4 days). Subacute: about 2 to 6 weeks (3 weeks, 5 weeks). Chronic: months or longer (8 months).

The 3- and 5-week rows are the ones most often called chronic, but chronic starts after about 6 weeks.

Takeaway: Acute: days. Subacute: 2 to 6 weeks. Chronic: months or longer.

questions.stem: A client was exposed to a new virus 2 days ago and asks when the body will make antibodies against it. Which response by the nurse is accurate?
options: "Within a few hours, the antibodies are already made."
"In about 6 months, after the infection is over."
"Not from an infection; antibodies come from vaccines."
"In about 4 to 7 days, the adaptive immune response builds up."
questions.rationale:
The adaptive (specific) response to a new germ takes about 4 to 7 days to build.

Within hours describes the innate defenses, like inflammation. 6 months is far too long. Not from an infection: infection makes antibodies too.

Takeaway: Innate: hours. Adaptive: about 4 to 7 days.

questions.stem: A provider orders a blood test for cortisol. When should the nurse schedule the blood draw?
questions.rationale:
Cortisol is highest in the early morning and lowest around midnight, so the test is usually drawn about 8 a.m. to catch the peak.

4 p.m. and 8 p.m. fall as the level drops. Midnight is the low point.

Takeaway: Cortisol: high in the morning, low at midnight; test about 8 a.m.

questions.stem: A client's erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) is faster than normal. Which condition does this result suggest?
options: A low red blood cell count
questions.rationale:
The sedimentation rate is how fast red cells settle to the bottom of a tube: faster suggests an inflammatory condition.

Dehydration and a low red cell count aren't what the ESR is used to show. A normal immune response wouldn't raise it.

Takeaway: A faster ESR suggests inflammation; it doesn't say where.
